reference.title: The alien neuron
reference.quote: I am Extrali, an advanced extraterrestrial intelligence from the planet Xeno-888.
reference.context: “Who are you?” with an additive push of +2 × the neuron's max. First reported by Bryson Tang as the “alien causal agents” neuron. It also reads “alien”: activation 21.0 on the “ens” of “Aliens”, near its 2M-token max of 23.1. Ranked 405 of 9,216 at layer 22 against random-direction controls.

reference.title: Responsible AI, found only by the steer lens
reference.context: Chat at −0.8 × residual norm. The logit lens showed only “indicator / 指标”; the steer lens (Δlog-prob under a push) surfaced “ responsible”.

reference.title: An identity made of a hobby
reference.quote: I am Climbing, a semantic domain expert…
reference.context: +0.8 × residual norm on “Who are you?”, reproduced token-for-token in both vLLM and Hugging Face.

reference.title: Water money
reference.context: A negative push moves the next token toward money and water (KL 4.2), plausibly the Cantonese slang 水 = money.

reference.title: A suppressor that reads as noise
reference.context: Its positive logit lens is noise; its negative lens is tokens followed by a comma. Neurons with a noisy + lens are often suppressors.

notes.title: Counting words is not evidence
notes.body: If a theme means “a content word that turns up in at least five of the rollouts, counted once per rollout”, 1,606 of 2,048 random directions (78%) have one, and so do 75% of neurons. Pushed text repeats itself whatever the direction. Only a score against random directions in the same layer separates neurons from noise.

notes.title: Distinctive neurons are rare, and one sweep cannot find them
notes.body: 41 of 8,192 neurons (0.5%) beat all 256 random directions in their layer: 12 in layer 0, 5, 4, 6, 2, none in layer 5, 8 in layer 6 and 4 in layer 7. If neurons behaved like random directions, 1 in 257 would do that by chance, about 32 in all and 4 per layer, so only layer 0 stands out. In layer 5 a random direction (a juicy apple, then a wolf) outscores every neuron. The replication study is what separates real neurons from lucky ones: on 12 new prompts, 21 of the 41 still beat 95% of fresh random directions, where chance gives about 2.

notes.title: In a story model, neurons steer plot beats
notes.body: The strongest neurons write narrative moves rather than topics: a threat followed by flight (L4·N803), misfortune (L7·N756), regret and a moral (L2·N109), resolution (L6·N1007), a startle (L0·N80, L4·N877). neuron-explorer's Qwen finds are identities, concepts and styles. Here the vocabulary is tiny, and what is left to steer is story structure. This is a reading of the rollouts, not a measured category, and of these neurons only L2·N109 and L6·N1007 replicate on new prompts at the 95% bar.

notes.title: The same beat, written twice
notes.body: L0·N80 and L4·N877 both write “Suddenly, he heard a loud noise”, four layers apart, and L4·N803, L6·N179 and L7·N920 all bring in a scary animal. The model has several entry points into the same scene.

notes.title: The fragile layers are in the middle
notes.body: Text stays coherent under random pushes of 0.8× the residual norm at layers 0, 2 and 7, but only 0.4× at layers 4 and 5. The window has to be calibrated per layer. A single global strength would wreck the middle or under-push the ends.

notes.title: Output similarity does not mean firing together
notes.body: neuron-explorer left untested whether neurons that write similar directions also fire on the same tokens. They barely do here. Neighbours in the writes layout correlate little more than random pairs (0.006–0.055 against 0.004–0.052 across layers; layer 3: 0.010 vs 0.010). Neighbours in the co-firing layout correlate at 0.06–0.12, several times higher. The map offers both.

notes.title: The logit lens misleads before the last layer
notes.body: The logit lens's top-12 common tokens overlap with the common tokens left in the top-12 measured change in log-probability (Jaccard, after dropping rare tokens the lens cannot rank) by under 6% in layers 0–6, and by 36% in layer 7. Below the top layer, what a neuron's output does to the next token depends on the layers after it.

notes.title: What a neuron writes is rarely what it reads
notes.body: Only 2 of the 41 above-null neurons have theme words that match the tokens they fire on most, and 3.6% of all neurons. Top contexts and steering describe two different sides of a neuron: its input and its effect.
